strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and under-explored problem: Anytime Neural Architecture Search (NAS) tailored specifically for tabular data.

The introduction of NAS-Bench-Tabular, which evaluates 160,000 unique architectures across three real-world tabular datasets, is a substantial contribution that can greatly benefit the AutoML and tabular deep learning communities.

The proposed zero-cost proxy, ExpressFlow, is theoretically grounded, combining trainability and expressivity by leveraging neuron saliency and layer-wise trajectory calibration. It achieves significantly higher Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficients (SRCC) than existing vision-centric proxies on tabular data.

The two-phase filtering-and-refinement framework with a budget-aware coordinator (ATLAS) is well-designed. It cleanly handles different time budgets and achieves outstanding anytime performance and search speedups (up to 82.75x).
The manuscript is exceptionally well-structured, with comprehensive ablation studies on hyper-parameters, initialization methods, batch sizes, and noise sensitivity provided in the appendices.
weaknesses: The search space is restricted to simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) architectures, where only the layer sizes (widths) are searched. Modern tabular deep learning often employs more complex architectures (such as FT-Transformer, TabNet, SAINT); evaluating or searching over these architectures would make the framework even more convincing.

In Equation 1 and the surrounding text, the computation of the trajectory length $\ell(z^l)$ is not fully explained in the main body. Given that this is a key calibration factor for the zero-cost proxy, a brief explanation of how it is calculated at initialization (without full training) would improve clarity.

Section G.4 demonstrates that ExpressFlow can work in a data-agnostic manner using an all-one vector. While this is computationally efficient, it raises the question of whether ExpressFlow is primarily capturing structural properties (depth and width) of the network rather than data-specific interactions. A brief discussion on how ATLAS adapts to different dataset characteristics under this data-agnostic setting would be valuable.

The paper would benefit from a baseline comparison against standard non-deep learning tabular models (such as XGBoost or LightGBM) to contextualize the absolute performance of the searched architectures.

strengths: Introduction of the anytime NAS formulation to tabular data, which is highly practical for cloud-based or resource-constrained environments.

Release of NAS-Bench-Tabular, a comprehensive benchmark containing 160,000 fully trained architectures over three real-world tabular datasets, which provides a valuable resource for the NAS community.

Proposal of ExpressFlow, a novel training-free zero-cost proxy tailored for tabular data that shows a high Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient (SRCC) with actual validation AUC, outperforming several existing proxies.
The proposed ATLAS framework achieves significant speedups (up to 82.75x) compared to standard training-based NAS while providing robust anytime capabilities.
weaknesses: The search space is limited to finding the optimal layer widths of a standard 4-layer MLP. This is a very simplified search space compared to the wide variety of modern deep tabular architectures (e.g., FT-Transformer, TabNet, ResNet-like tabular models). It is unclear how well the findings and the ExpressFlow proxy generalize to more complex topological search spaces.

There is a lack of clarity regarding how the trajectory length $\ell(z^l)$ is computed in practice. In Raghu et al. (2017), trajectory length is calculated along a specific input trajectory curve. The paper does not specify how this input curve or the corresponding trajectory is constructed and computed for tabular data at initialization, which hinders reproducibility.

The evaluation is restricted to only three datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo). Performance of deep learning models on tabular data is highly dataset-dependent, and typical tabular deep learning benchmarks evaluate on a much larger suite of datasets (e.g., from OpenML) to establish generalizability.

There is no comparison with standard tree-based models (such as tuned XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost). Showing how the searched MLP architectures compare in performance and efficiency to these traditional state-of-the-art tabular models would greatly strengthen the practical justification of the method.

strengths: The paper addresses anytime neural architecture search (NAS) on tabular data, which is an interesting and practically relevant direction given the resource constraints of cloud computing.
The authors construct and plan to release a benchmark dataset, NAS-Bench-Tabular, containing 160,000 MLP architectures with trained performance metrics.
The idea of a hybrid filtering-and-refinement framework to leverage both zero-cost proxies and progressive training-based evaluation (Successive Halving) is conceptually sound.
weaknesses: Critical Lack of Clarity and Reproducibility on Trajectory Length: The key component of the proposed ExpressFlow proxy is the recalibration weight containing the trajectory length $\ell(z^l)$ of the $l$-th layer. However, the manuscript completely fails to explain how $\ell(z^l)$ is numerically computed for an arbitrary architecture at initialization. While Eq (1) and the text mention a path integral definition from Raghu et al. (2017) parameterized by $t$, the paper states that ExpressFlow requires only a single forward and backward pass (1FC+1BC). Computing the actual trajectory length of a neural network layer requires numerical integration over an input path (multiple forward passes). If a theoretical approximation or constant was used instead, it is never defined. This is a severe reproducibility and clarity issue.

Mathematical Discrepancies: There is a major contradiction in how ExpressFlow is defined. In Eq (1) on page 5, ExpressFlow includes the width and trajectory length recalibration weights ($K_l / \ell(z^l)$). However, in Eq (12) in the appendix, as well as in Table 13 (which summarizes all proxies), the ExpressFlow score $s_a$ is defined as the unweighted sum $\sum_n |\partial L / \partial z_n| \odot z_n$. The theoretical analysis in Appendix G.3 only applies to this unweighted version, leaving the weighted version used in the experiments mathematically unjustified and confusingly presented.

Simplistic Search Space (HPO vs. NAS): The search space is extremely simple, only varying the layer sizes of a 4-layer vanilla MLP. In contemporary machine learning, tuning the hidden dimension sizes of a feedforward network is considered Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO), not Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Real tabular NAS should search over topological options, skip connections, or operations specialized for tabular data (e.g., attention blocks, feature interactions as in TabNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT). It is an overstatement to call this "Anytime NAS on Tabular Data."

Flatness of the Search Space: According to Section 4.1.1, the median architecture on Frappe has an AUC of 0.9772, while the global optimum is 0.9814. On Criteo, the median is 0.8014 and the optimum is 0.8033. Since the difference between a random architecture (median) and the absolute best architecture is negligible (less than 0.4% AUC on Criteo), the search space is remarkably flat. This severely diminishes the practical significance of designing complex anytime search algorithms for this space, as a simple default or random MLP would perform almost optimally.

Missing Tabular and HPO Baselines: Since the paper targets tabular data, it is crucial to compare the searched architectures with standard tabular baselines such as GBDTs (XGBoost, LightGBM) or state-of-the-art tabular deep models (FT-Transformer). If a default XGBoost outperforms the best searched 4-layer MLP, the utility of the method is limited. Furthermore, since the problem is essentially HPO, the authors should have compared their framework against state-of-the-art multi-fidelity and anytime HPO baselines (such as PASHA or advanced BOHB variants).
